How Scoring Works

Fantasy 365 is a best-ball league — there are no weekly lineups, no waivers, and no decisions to make once you're drafted. Everything you own scores automatically, all year, based on real results.

Teams

Every team you draft — NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, NCAAF, NCAAB, MLS, or EPL — scores the exact same way, in two parts:

  • Regular Season — the better their record, the more points. A perfect regular season is worth up to 10 points.
  • Final Result — how far they go in the playoffs, up to winning it all. Worth up to another 10 points.

So an undefeated regular season plus a championship can score up to 20 points total. You can own more than one team from the same league if you want — there's no per-league cap — but you get one required spot per league plus 4 extra "flex" team spots shared across all 8 leagues.

Players

Most positions work on the same simple idea: the better a player performs compared to everyone else drafted at that position, the more points you get. You draft 2 players at most positions, but only the better of the two actually counts — that's the "best-ball" part.

  • NFL (QB / RB / WR) — ranked by non-PPR fantasy points against everyone else drafted at that same position.
  • NBA (Guard / Forward / Center) — ranked by standard fantasy points against everyone else drafted at that same position.
  • NHL (Skaters) — ranked by Goals + Assists against everyone else drafted at that position.
  • MLB — split into Hitters and Pitchers, ranked by Batting Average, Home Runs, and Pitcher Score, plus 2 flexible bench spots that can be either. Shohei Ohtani is the one exception on the whole board — he can fill either a hitter or a pitcher spot.
  • Golf — only the 4 major championships count (Masters, PGA Championship, U.S. Open, Open Championship). Nothing else all year matters for scoring. You draft 2 golfers; the better one counts.
  • Tennis — only the 4 Grand Slams count. You draft 2 tennis players (any mix of ATP/WTA); at each Slam, whichever of the two goes furthest is the one that scores.

Most scoring categories max out at 10 points — Batting Average and Home Runs are capped a little lower, at 8 each. MLB is actually three separate categories (Batting Average, Home Runs, and Pitcher Score), so a strong MLB roster can score more than 10 points combined if it's leading in more than one.

Specifics

Want the exact point breakdowns? Expand any section below.

Team — finish tiers

The Final Result half of team scoring (up to 10 points) is tiered by how far a team goes in the playoffs. The exact cutoffs vary slightly by league format, but the shape is the same across all 8:

  • Champion — 10
  • Runner-up — 6
  • Final 4 / Conference finalist — 4
  • Final 8 / Divisional round — 2
  • Other playoff qualifier — 1
  • Missed the playoffs — 0

Example: Two teams both make the playoffs. One loses in the first round (1 point). The other loses in the championship game (6 points) — same "made the playoffs" starting point, very different payoff for going further.

Player — NFL

Non-PPR fantasy points: 0.04 per passing yard, 4 per passing TD, -1 per interception, 0.1 per rushing/receiving yard, 6 per rushing/receiving TD, 2 per 2-point conversion, -2 per fumble lost. No points-per-reception.

Your best QB, RB, and WR are each ranked against every other drafted player at that position:

  • 1st — 10
  • 2nd — 9
  • 3rd — 8
  • 4th — 7
  • 5th — 6
  • 6th–8th — 4
  • 9th–11th — 2
  • 12th–15th — 1
  • 16th or lower — 0

Example: You draft 2 QBs. Across the league, 20 QBs are drafted total. Your better QB finishes with the 3rd-most fantasy points among all 20 — that's 8 points for you, and your other QB's stats don't matter at all.

Player — NBA

Ranked by cumulative standard fantasy points across the season. Your best Guard, Forward, and Center are each ranked against every other drafted player at that position:

  • 1st — 10
  • 2nd — 9
  • 3rd — 8
  • 4th — 7
  • 5th — 6
  • 6th–8th — 4
  • 9th–12th — 2
  • 13th–20th — 1
  • 21st or lower — 0
Player — NHL

Ranked by regular-season Goals + Assists. Your best skater is ranked against every other drafted skater:

  • 1st — 10
  • 2nd — 9
  • 3rd — 8
  • 4th — 7
  • 5th — 6
  • 6th–8th — 4
  • 9th–11th — 2
  • 12th–15th — 1
  • 16th or lower — 0
Player — MLB

Pitcher Score formula: +1 per out recorded, +3 per strikeout, +5 per quality start, +5 per win, -1 per hit allowed, -0.5 per walk, -3 per earned run. Batting Average and Home Runs use the raw stat itself.

All 3 categories are ranked separately against every other qualifying player drafted — but Batting Average and Home Runs top out lower than everything else in the league:

Batting Average and Home Runs (max 8 each):

  • 1st — 8
  • 2nd — 7
  • 3rd — 6
  • 4th–5th — 5
  • 6th–8th — 3
  • 9th–12th — 2
  • 13th–20th — 1
  • 21st or lower — 0

Pitcher Score (max 10):

  • 1st — 10
  • 2nd — 9
  • 3rd — 8
  • 4th — 7
  • 5th — 6
  • 6th–8th — 4
  • 9th–12th — 2
  • 13th–20th — 1
  • 21st or lower — 0

Example: Your MLB roster has the league's best qualified batting average (8 points) and the 3rd-most home runs (6 points) — that's 14 points from hitting alone, before your pitcher's score is even counted.

Player — Golf

Golf scoring happens in 3 steps, all based purely on how a golfer finishes at each of the 4 majors:

Step 1 — base points per major, by finish:

  • Champion — 16
  • Runner-up — 12
  • 3rd — 10
  • 4th–5th — 8
  • 6th–10th — 6
  • 11th–20th — 4
  • 21st–30th — 2
  • Made the cut, 31st or lower — 1
  • Missed the cut / didn't play — 0

Step 2 — each major gets weighted differently:

  • Masters — ×1.25
  • U.S. Open — ×1.15
  • Open Championship — ×1.10
  • PGA Championship — ×1.00

All 4 weighted major scores are added together into one season-long ranking for every golfer.

Step 3 — that ranking converts into your actual league points:

  • 1st — 15
  • 2nd — 13
  • 3rd — 12
  • 4th — 10
  • 5th — 9
  • 6th–8th — 7
  • 9th–12th — 4
  • 13th–16th — 2
  • 17th–20th — 1
  • 21st or lower — 0

That 15-point ceiling is higher than the usual 10-point cap elsewhere — golf is intentionally the highest-risk, highest-reward category.

Example: Say your golfer finishes runner-up at the Masters (12 × 1.25 = 15), 6th-10th at the PGA Championship (6 × 1.00 = 6), misses the cut at the U.S. Open (0 × 1.15 = 0), and finishes 3rd at the Open Championship (10 × 1.10 = 11). That's 15 + 6 + 0 + 11 = 32 weighted points for the season — good enough for 2nd place across the whole league, which converts to 13 league points.

Player — Tennis

At each of the 4 Grand Slams, whichever of your 2 tennis players goes furthest earns you points for that Slam:

  • Champion — 5
  • Runner-up — 3.5
  • Semifinal — 2
  • Quarterfinal — 1
  • Earlier than that — 0

Add up all 4 Slams for a max possible 20 points on the year.

Example: Your pick wins Wimbledon (5 points) but loses in the first round of the other 3 Slams (0 each) — that's still 5 points total for the year. One deep run is what matters; early exits elsewhere don't subtract anything.
